Area Forecast Discussion...UPDATED
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
909 AM EST Fri Nov 20 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
The latest ensembles have shifted the axis of heavy rainfall
late this weekend a bit more to the east. However, model
solutions continue to waffle back and forth which indicates the
level of uncertainty that remains in the forecast.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Dry and mild conditions expected to continue through 
  Saturday.

- 2) Forecast remains uncertain as a coastal low tracks up the
  Eastern Seaboard Sunday into Monday, followed by a cool down.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and mild conditions expected to continue 
through Saturday.

Like much of this week, sunshine will again be abundant with 
high pressure in charge one more day. 850-mb temperatures rise 
to around 8C which carries forecast highs to around the 70 
degree mark. Gradients remain weak which supports light and 
variable winds through the day. Heading into the tonight, expect
clouds to increase from south to north given the approach from 
low pressure from the southeastern U.S. This yields a bump up in
low temperatures with most in the mid 30s to low 40s.

The start of the weekend carries one more dry day, but with
increased cloud cover. High pressure gradually retreats into New
England while an inverted trough along the coast approaches from
the south. The shift in the surface pattern favors easterly
onshore gradients. Forecast highs drop off by around 2 to 5
degrees, but this is still above average for the time of year.
Any potential for rain holds off until late Saturday night, if
not a bit longer. Nighttime lows are set to fall into the 40s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Forecast remains uncertain as a coastal low tracks 
up the Eastern Seaboard Sunday into Monday, followed by a cool
down.

An area of low pressure is forecast to develop off the Southeast 
U.S. coast late this week, then track northward along the coast this 
weekend. The low's initial forward speed is going to be slow as it 
gets trapped underneath a brief, weak upper ridge, then quickly 
picks up speed as it moves northeast with a strong upper trough 
approaching from the OH Valley. There remains considerable 
differences among the global guidance, both run to run and between 
models in each run. The ensemble guidance for both the European and 
GFS remain quite dispersive with low tracks well inland across the 
NC/VA Piedmont to well offshore of the Mid-Atlantic. 

There continues to be too much uncertainty to pin down any specific 
details or impacts to our area. Rain chances Sunday into Sunday 
night continue to slowly increase, especially east of the Blue Ridge 
with the highest certainty east of I-95. The exact track of the low 
is going to be critical to where the heaviest rain falls, though 
there could be a sharp gradient on the western side of the precip 
shield from heavy to very light rain amounts. It is worth mentioning 
the higher-end of the ensemble spread indicates 2-4" as a worst-case 
scenario, but many members also have little to no rain for most of 
the area - this probably speak the best to how much uncertainty 
remains. The location of the heaviest QPF also varies greatly from 
along US-15 to the Delmarva. Continue to monitor the forecast over 
the next few days as guidance hopefully starts to converge on a 
solution for this weekend. 

A strong Canadian high builds across much of the central to 
eastern CONUS during the early part of next week. This is going 
to bring us dry, brisk, and much colder conditions. 

Another trough is progged to move across the Ohio Valley Wednesday 
through Friday next week. Depending on your model or ensemble of 
choice, a low may develop and bring widespread precip to the area. 
Colder solutions do favor snow in the mountains of the
Alleghenies.

&&

.AVIATION /14Z FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
VFR conditions likely continue through the first half of the
weekend. High pressure sticks around through tonight before
retreating back into New England. Gradients remain weak in
response before winds shift to easterly onshore flow by
Saturday.

Approaching low pressure from the southeastern U.S. coast will
favor restrictions on Sunday into Sunday night. There is likely
to be a sharp west-east gradients in impacts, but low clouds
should support a mixture of IFR to MVFR ceilings. This is
accompanied by a breezy north to northeasterly wind with gusts
up to around 20 knots on Sunday.

Improvements return by Monday as a cold front to the west moves
through early in the day. VFR conditions are expected both
Monday and Tuesday with prevailing winds shifting from
northwesterly over to northerly. Daytime gusts each day begin to
approach 20 to 25 knots.

&&

.MARINE...
Tranquil conditions continue over the waterways owing to
persistent high pressure and the associated weak gradients. This
is expected to continue through late Saturday before the
influence of low pressure near the southeastern U.S. favors a
return to advisory caliber winds. North to northeasterly winds
on Sunday will likely require Small Craft Advisories, possibly
higher depending on the track and placement of the coastal low.

A cold front off to the west moves through early Monday which
favors another round of increasing wind fields. This brings
northwesterlies on Monday before shifting to northerly by
Tuesday. Each day favors marine wind gusts to around 20 to 25
knots which suggests additional advisories are likely.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...
High pressure will remain over the area through late tonight 
before moving off to the northeast Saturday into Sunday. While 
winds will stay on the lighter side through Saturday, RH values 
remain low each day. Overnight recoveries, especially on the 
ridges, will be very poor as well with RH values averaging in the
40s to 50s. Expect afternoon RH values to drop well into the 20s 
today west of U.S. 15 and south of I-66, with mainly upper 20s to 
30s values elsewhere. This dry air mass will also be paired with 
seasonably warm temperatures, so this will really act to dry out 
already very dry fuels. While any fires will be slow to move due 
to lack of wind, very dry air will make for easy fire starts, so 
exercise extreme caution through Saturday. 

Not helping matters is that there is no precipitation expected 
east of the Appalachians through Saturday. An area of low 
pressure lifting northward from the southeastern U.S. coast is set
to bring a soaking rain to portions of the area on Sunday into 
Monday. The overall confidence for ample rainfall continues to 
increase, but there is still immense uncertainty in the low track.
Based on the latest forecast package, forecast rainfall amounts 
through Monday morning are 0.50 to 1.50 inches east of the Blue 
Ridge, with mainly 0.10 to 0.50 inches off to the west. As this 
system begins to impact the region, relative humidities come up 
significantly which will temporarily halt the drying of fine 
fuels.

Colder and drier air returns early next week before another
possible system impacts the region close to the Thanksgiving
holiday.
